What Makes an API RESTful

Resources identified by URLs, no server-rendered views, and no session driving what a request means.

You've built CRUD in Laravel already — routes, controllers, a database — but web.php routes and the API this project builds aren't quite the same shape. The difference is REST (Representational State Transfer): a style for designing APIs around a small set of rules, rather than a framework feature. It's worth naming explicitly now, since the very next topic will describe this project's routes as "RESTful" and lean on the term.

Three ideas matter most for this API:

  • Everything is a resource, identified by a URL. A ticket is a resource; the collection of all tickets lives at /tickets, and one ticket lives at /tickets/:id. Compare that to a typical Laravel web route like /tickets/5/edit, where edit names an action, not a resource — REST avoids verbs in the URL, because the next idea already covers "what to do to a resource."
  • The HTTP method says what to do to that resource, not the URL. GET /tickets/5 reads it; the next topic covers the rest of the verbs. This is covered in full on the next slide.
  • No server-rendered views, and no server-side session driving the request. A Laravel web route typically returns a Blade view, and can rely on session state (e.g. "the logged-in user," flash messages) built up across requests. This API instead returns JSON only, and — for now, before auth exists in Week 4 — every request is handled from scratch, with nothing about it stored server-side between requests. That property is called statelessness: each request carries everything needed to handle it, rather than depending on something the server remembers from an earlier one.

None of this requires Express specifically — it's a design convention any framework, or no framework at all, could follow. Express just happens to make it easy to build APIs this way, which the next topic starts putting into practice.
